Here’s my summary. There are two widely used ways of training Transformers. One is autoregressive training. We generally use this when we want to train a model to generate sequences of words, one by one. This means that the model is being trained to predict the next token/word given the previous tokens.

So when a model gets a sequence of length N during training, it’s making N predictions; one for the first token (using none of the sequence as input), one for the second token given only the first, one for the third token given the first and second, and so on. So for each prediction, the model’s input is constrained so that it doesn’t contain the “answer.” (As an aside, autoregressive training is used for an entire class of statistical modes called generative models, and is not transformer-specific.
Of course the transformer can be trained in the way we train an RNN (one token after another with teacher forcing, i.e., the autoregressive fashion).

snippets: Autoregressive Transformer models have demonstrated impressive performance in video generation, but their sequential token-by-token decoding process poses a major bottleneck, particularly for long videos represented by tens of thousands of tokens. In this paper, we propose Diagonal Decoding (DiagD), a training-free inference acceleration algorithm for autoregressively pre-trained models that exploits spatial and temporal correlations in videos.

In this paper, we focus on autoregressive Transformers, as they have demonstrated performance on par with diffusion models [20, 44], while inheriting key advantages from large language models, such as zero-shot in-context learning [46], long-range generation capabilities [24], and the ability to smoothly integrate multiple modalities [20].

Compared with diffusion models, autoregressive Transformers exhibit unique features as shown in the blooming of Large Language Models (LLMs) [31, 5] in recent years, including zero-shot emergent in-context learning capabilities [46], and scaling laws [18, 30]. Leveraging architectures similar to LLMs enables vision models to inherit these advancements and naturally extend to multi-modal inputs.

Additionally, autoregressive models can generate videos of arbitrary length in a streaming paradigm, which is challenging for most of the diffusion models. However, the video generation models usually utilize a visual tokenizer [9, 33] to transform raw videos to tens of thousands of tokens, which poses a significant bottleneck for autoregressive models that generate tokens sequentially, especially when generating high-resolution, long-duration videos.
